en.title: Sony says ‘reasonable consumers’ know they don’t own the digital games they buy
en.description: It’s “not plausible” to suggest people believe they’re “obtaining ownership”, it says
en.fullContent:
It’s “not plausible” to suggest people believe they’re “obtaining ownership”, it says

Sony has told a court that “reasonable consumers” are fully aware that when they buy a digital game, that doesn’t mean they own it.

In June, four players sued Sony Interactive Entertainment for allegedly breaking California law by not making it clear on the PlayStation Store that players are buying licences to games, not actually owning the games.

The argument made was that because the PlayStation Store uses terms like “Buy Now” and “Confirm Purchase”, players are under the impression they’re buying a copy of a game that they then own, rather than a licence to access the game which can be revoked by Sony at any point in the future.

Now, as reported by Game File, Sony recently filed its response to the lawsuit, claiming that customers are not only told “your purchase of this digital product amounts to a licence”, but that “reasonable consumers” already understand this anyway without having to be told.

Sony’s argument is that because digital copies of games are not a finite resource, and that because multiple people can buy a digital copy of the same game, that means nobody actually ‘owns’ it – if they did, nobody else would be able to have it.

en.title: Gems, ghosts and GTA VI: the biggest video games for autumn 2026
en.description: There are juggernauts and indie gems aplenty for when the nights draw in, from an ingenious puzzle game to blockbusters such as Marvel’s Wolverine ...
en.fullContent:
There are juggernauts and indie gems aplenty for when the nights draw in, from an ingenious puzzle game to blockbusters such as Marvel’s Wolverine and Call of Duty
  See all of our unmissable autumn arts recommendations here

After 20 years away, Capcom’s hyper kinetic action adventure returns, pitting skilled samurai Miyamoto Musashi against hordes of warriors and demons in Edo-period Kyoto. Master the complex combat then prepare for flashing blades, disembodied limbs and geysers of spraying blood.
  4 September; PC, PS5, Switch 2, Xbox

Billed as the first ever 5D platformer, Screenbound has you navigating a 3D landscape while simultaneously playing an on-screen handheld console, which contains a 2D mirror world. Everything you do in one affects the other in mind-bending ways. The most ingenious puzzle game we’ve seen in a long time.
  10 September; PC, PS5, Xbox

The team behind the brilliant Marvel’s Spider-Man titles is back with a very different kind of hero. The open-world New York setting is gone in favour of a globe-trotting narrative following Logan on his quest to protect vulnerable mutants. The visuals are gorgeous, while the slick combat brings literal meaning to the term bleeding edge.
  15 September; PS5

The tactical role-playing adventure series returns to the realm explored in the acclaimed Fire Emblem: Three Houses. This time, hopeful contestants arrive at the glorious city of Dagsion to compete in a contest where the winner is granted a single wish. Deep combat, lush settings and fraught relationships are guaranteed.
   17 September; Switch 2

Silent Hill comes to the east coast of Scotland in a beautifully gloomy new horror adventure. You play as Simon Ordell, returning to a quiet harbour town with no memory of whatever catastrophe has taken place there. The place seems abandoned, but you are not alone for long …
  24 September; PC, PS5

en.title: Sony is telling PlayStation customers they don’t own the digital video games they paid $70 for
en.description: Just because PlayStation customers “purchased” video games on the console doesn’t mean they actually own the games, or so says the gaming console’s...
en.fullContent:
Just because PlayStation customers “purchased” video games on the console doesn’t mean they actually own the games, or so says the gaming console’s parent company, Sony.

The Japan-based electronics, movie, and gaming giant is facing a class action lawsuit filed in California’s Northern District Court in June, in which four customers allege that the technology giant did not properly disclose that paying for a downloadable game does not grant permanent ownership or access to it. The lawsuit claims Sony’s disclosures violate a 2024 California law AB 2426 requiring a warning that “states in plain language that ‘buying’ or ‘purchasing’ the digital good is a license.”

Two of the plaintiffs bought Resident Evil Requiem, per the motion to dismiss. Sony argued that because two of them purchased the same game just 11 days apart, that means no reasonable consumer can assume they owned exclusive rights to a digital copy, given how anyone could buy the same “copy” at any given time.The company’s filing states it’s simply “not plausible” that customers believed they owned the games outright.

In the motion to dismiss, Sony argued it made clear in its terms of service and end user license agreement that its digital games are purchased, not owned.

“A reasonable user would have seen the terms of service above or directly below the action button, the user unambiguously manifested assent to the terms of service, including the arbitration provision, and the terms and arbitration provision were valid and binding,” the motion said.

Sony isn’t the only video game seller responding to AB 2426. In January, GameStop customer Jake Weber sued the gaming store for allegedly violating the California law. The complaint includes a screenshot of a store page for Pokémon Legends: Arceus, noting that the page does not include information about customers purchasing a license for the game, and not the actual game. The lawsuit is ongoing. Online PC game marketplace Steam, on the other hand, began including a warning on its shopping cart page telling customers they are buying a license to a particular game that could be revoked in the future.

en.title: GTA 6 extended look reaches 31.1m views on Netflix in four days, making it the most-viewed title last week
en.description: The 30-minute preview was listed under Netflix's English-language films, ranking No. 1 in 87 of 93 countries tracked by the platform
en.fullContent:
The 30-minute preview was listed under Netflix's English-language films, ranking No. 1 in 87 of 93 countries tracked by the platform

The extended look of Grand Theft Auto 6  was the most-viewed title on Netflix last week, reaching 31.1 million views in four days.

As  Variety reports, viewership was tracked from the premiere last Thursday (August 27) through Sunday (August 30), which marks the end of Netflix's weekly Top 10 viewing window.

The 30-minute preview led Netflix's English-language film list in 87 of 93 tracked countries, surpassing the crime thriller The Whisper Man, which stars Robert De Niro and Adam Scott.

The premiere was exclusive to Netflix for six hours before becoming available  on YouTube. The video on Rockstar Games' channel has since reached 17 million views.

Variety noted that Netflix "defines a view as the total hours viewed for a title divided by its runtime, meaning one household watching a program twice would only be counted once." In contrast, YouTube counts a view as soon as a video begins to play.

en.title: Christopher Judge Explains Why He's Not In The God Of War TV Show
en.description: The casting of Kratos for Amazon’s God of War TV show has been a roller coaster ride. With the adaptation suddenly swapping from Ryan Hurst to Dave...
en.fullContent:
The casting of Kratos for Amazon’s God of War TV show has been a roller coaster ride. With the adaptation suddenly swapping from Ryan Hurst to Dave Bautista for the lead role, it’s understandable that fans would wonder why Christopher Judge, who plays Kratos in the modern games, seemingly isn’t playing the character in the show.

“With Ryan, I thought that was absolutely the right choice. He’s played all the games,” Judge told Collider during a recent Fan Expo Canada panel. “He’s a gamer and new father; like, who better? Then when he got hurt, it was like, are they going to take time to read with and call people back? So when I heard the name of Bautista, I thought, ‘Didn’t he just lose like 100 pounds?’ So I hope he’s going to be great. I think he’s going to be great. I just hope it doesn’t cause any health issues to put back on all that weight.”

The co-star of Stargate SG-1 went on to explain that, being in his early 60s, the physical tax involved in portraying a literal god in live action isn’t something he wants to contend with. “I didn’t want to do it,” Judge said. “I didn’t want to, at 62 years old, work 16-to-18-hour days. I didn’t want to be dieting constantly; I didn’t want to be working out constantly.” He briefly changed his mind when talking to his grandson and began working out and reading for the role, but eventually pulled out of the running.

Judge continued, “We had talked, and I thought, ‘God, what a great legacy to leave for my grandson.’ So I started working out. I got bigger. Then, just the reality of it…because I did read! I did read for it. It was so hard for me to memorize my lines, which I never had a problem with. And that was my mind and body starting to tell me, ‘You don’t want to do this.’ I was one of the leads of Stargate at 33 to 44 and then stopped. Now, at 62, to be the lead, I just have no desire to live that way again.”

Fortunately for players, that doesn’t apply to video games. Sony Santa Monica already revealed that while God of War Laufey isn’t starring Kratos, another sequel already in development will bring the titular character back into the spotlight, and seemingly Judge along with it. In the meantime, the God of War TV show will have to begin reshooting the episodes that were already finished with Bautista taking Hurst’s place, so who knows how long it will be until the series actually begins to air.
